questions.question: Scenario: You work for a careers service advising school leavers. You have been asked to explain what the hospitality industry offers as a career. Required: produce a one-page information sheet with headed sections covering (i) the three sectors of the industry with an example of each, (ii) three job roles and the area of the business each belongs to, and (iii) the benefits of working in hospitality. [10]
questions.model_answer:
Paper 2-A marks the document format, so produce a titled information sheet with the three headings asked for and bullets beneath each.

(i) The three sectors. Commercial, which exists to make a profit and is paid for by the customer, for example a hotel or restaurant. Voluntary, which exists to help people rather than to profit and is funded by donations, for example a charity soup kitchen or a mosque langar. Public, which is funded by government, for example catering in a state school or hospital.

(ii) Job roles by area. Kitchen or back of house: commis chef, the junior chef learning the basics. Front of house: receptionist, who is the first person a guest meets. Management and support: events coordinator, who plans and runs functions. Front of house means staff a guest can see; back of house means those they usually cannot.

(iii) Benefits of working in hospitality. You learn the industry and improve customer-service skills. You build confidence and skills in problem-handling and negotiation. There are clear routes for progression, since a commis chef can rise to head chef. Hours can be flexible, which suits students, and the work is varied with international opportunities.

Name the outcome: a school leaver reading the sheet understands the range of the industry and can identify a realistic entry point.

questions.question: Scenario: A guest at the Cedar Hotel has told reception that her son has a severe nut allergy. The waiter takes the order but does not pass the information to the kitchen, and the dessert served contains almond paste. The boy has a reaction and an ambulance is called. Required: as duty manager, explain what went wrong, and set out the steps you will take to make sure it cannot happen again. [10]
questions.model_answer:
Spot: allergy information was taken at reception but never reached the kitchen, so a life-threatening allergen was served to the guest who declared it.

Cite: every customer shares three basic needs, to feel welcome, to feel safe and to receive value, and safety is the one that was broken here. Customers with dietary needs require accurate allergen information, and the business has a legal duty to provide it.

Apply: the failure was in communication rather than in the kitchen's cooking. There was no written record passed from reception to the waiter to the chef, no check at the point of ordering, and no final check before the dessert left the pass.

Steps to prevent recurrence. Record every allergy in writing on the booking and on the order ticket, not verbally. Require the waiter to repeat the allergy back to the guest and to the kitchen, and to confirm it at the pass before serving. Keep a current allergen matrix for every dish on the menu, available to all staff. Train all staff, including casual staff, on the fourteen named allergens and on what to do if a reaction occurs. Cover this in the pre-service briefing whenever an allergy booking is expected. Review the incident with the whole team without blaming an individual, because a blame culture makes staff hide mistakes.

Name the outcome: allergy information becomes impossible to lose because it is written and checked three times, and the hotel avoids both a repeat of the harm and the legal and reputational consequences.

questions.question: Scenario: At the Marina Restaurant, two chefs have stopped speaking to each other after an argument about who left a fridge door open. Other staff have begun taking sides, and service has slowed. Required: as head chef, produce a short action plan explaining how you will resolve the conflict and prevent it spreading. [8]
questions.model_answer:
Spot: an unresolved conflict between two chefs has grown into a split in the team, and it is now affecting service.

Cite: conflict is normal in a pressured kitchen, but it must be recognised and dealt with early, because negative relationships cause poor communication, mistakes, low morale and high staff turnover. Cliques and taking sides spread the problem to people who were not involved.

Apply and act, in order. First, deal with it now rather than hoping it settles, because the longer it runs the more staff are drawn in. Second, speak to each chef privately and separately, and listen to both accounts fully before forming a view. Third, stay neutral and keep the discussion on the behaviour and the facts, never on personality. Fourth, bring them together to agree a practical solution, which here means an agreed procedure for checking and closing the fridges and a shared responsibility rather than a search for who was at fault. Fifth, address the wider team briefly: make clear that taking sides is not acceptable and that the matter is closed. Sixth, set a date to review whether the agreement is holding. If the two still cannot work together, escalate to mediation and then, if necessary, to the formal grievance procedure.

Name the outcome: the immediate dispute is settled, the fridge risk is controlled by a procedure rather than by blame, and the rest of the team sees that conflict is handled fairly, which discourages it in future.

questions.question: Scenario: You are the new kitchen supervisor at the Grand Palm Hotel. On your first shift you find warm rice sitting on the counter from lunch service four hours earlier, a probe thermometer that nobody has calibrated, and cooked chicken stored on the shelf below raw fish. Required: produce a briefing for the kitchen team identifying each hazard, the rule that has been broken, and the correct practice. [10]
questions.model_answer:
Present this as a headed briefing with one section per hazard.

Hazard 1, the warm rice. Spot: cooked rice has been left at room temperature for four hours. Cite: the danger zone is 5 C to 63 C, and cooked rice is a high-risk food in which Bacillus cereus multiplies and produces a heat-stable toxin. Apply: this rice must be discarded, not reheated, because reheating to 75 C kills the bacteria but not the toxin they have already produced. Correct practice: cool rice within 90 minutes, ideally in shallow trays or a blast chiller, then store at 0 C to 5 C, use within two to three days and reheat once only to 75 C or above. Name the outcome: if served, this rice would cause vomiting and illness within hours and could close the kitchen.

Hazard 2, the uncalibrated probe. Spot: no one can show when the thermometer was last checked. Cite: core cooking temperature of 75 C is a critical control point, and a control point is worthless if the instrument measuring it is wrong. Apply: calibrate the probe in iced water and boiling water, record the check, and clean and sanitise it between every use so it does not itself spread bacteria. Name the outcome: temperature records become evidence the business can rely on and show to an environmental health officer.

Hazard 3, storage order. Spot: cooked chicken is below raw fish. Cite: raw food must always be stored below ready-to-eat food. Apply: move all raw items to the bottom shelf immediately, with cooked and ready-to-eat food above, everything covered, labelled and dated. Name the outcome: juices from raw fish cannot drip onto food that will be eaten without further cooking, so cross-contamination is prevented.

Close the briefing with the standing rule: if in doubt, throw it out.

questions.question: Scenario: A hospital caterer has been asked to redesign the patient lunch menu. Many patients are elderly, some are recovering from surgery, and several have been assessed as underweight. Required: advise the caterer on how the menu should be planned, explaining your reasoning. [8]
questions.model_answer:
Spot: the menu must meet the needs of elderly patients, patients recovering from surgery, and patients who are underweight, which are three different nutritional situations served from one kitchen.

Cite: a balanced diet supplies all nutrient groups in the right proportions, and different groups have different requirements. Protein is needed for growth and the repair of tissue; carbohydrate supplies energy; vitamins and minerals such as calcium, iron and vitamin C support bone health, blood and healing; fibre and water keep digestion working.

Apply to these patients. Patients recovering from surgery need extra protein to repair tissue and vitamin C to support wound healing, so include eggs, fish, chicken, pulses and dairy, with fruit and vegetables at every meal. Underweight patients need energy-dense food in smaller portions rather than large plates they cannot finish, so use full-fat milk, add cheese or cream to soups and mashed potato, and offer nourishing snacks between meals. Elderly patients often have reduced appetite, difficulty chewing and a higher risk of dehydration and constipation, so offer soft, easy-to-chew options, moderate portions, adequate fibre and drinks with and between every meal, and pay attention to calcium and vitamin D for bone health. Practical points: keep salt moderate for blood pressure, present food attractively because appetite is affected by appearance, and offer choice so patients eat what they will actually finish. Record and respect all allergies, texture-modified requirements and religious or cultural needs such as halal and vegetarian options.

Name the outcome: patients eat more of what is served, recovery is supported rather than delayed by poor nutrition, and food waste falls because portions and textures match what patients can manage.

questions.question: Scenario: The Willow Cafe has opened in a town where most customers are families with young children, elderly residents, and workers wanting a quick lunch. The owner has designed one standard menu and service style for everyone. Required: advise the owner on how to meet the differing needs of these three customer groups. [6]
questions.model_answer:
Spot: three customer types with very different needs are being served by a single standard offer, so each group is partly unserved.

Cite: different customer types have different needs, but all customers share three basic needs, to feel welcome, to feel safe and to get value for money. Missing a specific need breaks one of the three basic ones.

Apply, group by group. Families with young children need a children's menu with smaller portions, high chairs, space for a pushchair, baby-changing facilities and quick service before children lose patience; safety matters, so hot drinks should not be placed within a child's reach. Elderly residents need accessible entry without steps, clear and larger print on the menu, good lighting, comfortable seating, unhurried service and staff with patience; softer options on the menu help those with difficulty chewing. Workers wanting a quick lunch need speed above all, so offer a clearly marked express menu, pre-prepared options, a takeaway service and fast card payment.

Name the outcome: each group finds what it came for, so all three return regularly rather than going elsewhere, and the cafe builds a customer base across the whole day instead of only at one peak.
